newsitem.title: USA: Lighter values keep rising as Zippo celebrates 65th year.
newsitem.headline: Lighter values keep rising as Zippo celebrates 65th year.

text.p: Joe Camel may be dead, but Zippo lives on, lighting up -- if not cigars and cigarettes -- the lives of a growing army of collectors.

The party is just beginning -- this weekend -- to celebrate the 65th anniversary of an American icon that began as a surefire, windproof way of lighting a cigarette in 1932, and soon became an artifact tracing American history up to the present.

Up to 10,000 collectors and spectators are expected to gather at Zippo's birthplace in Bradford, Pa., doubling the town's population, for a two-day bash that includes the opening of an official Zippo museum, a trade show and a musical extravaganza with tunes that have any "zip" or "light" in them.
Never mind that it's no longer cool to smoke. Or that 9-year-old Joe Camel, cartoon mascot for the Camel brand of cigarettes, was killed off this month under pressure from anti-smoking forces.
Collectors don't pay up to $10,000 for a Zippo to light up. Many don't even smoke.

"Zippo, to me, is the quintessence of America. A Zippo lighter is a canvas on which American history has been recorded," said David Poore, one of the lighter's biggest collectors and author of a book on the icon.

In a forward to the book, "Zippo: the Great American Light," Tim Ziaukas, assistant professor of public relations at the University of Pittsburgh at Bradford, said: "The lighters tell the tales of the great wars, as well as the images and trends, sometimes historic, sometimes kitschy, that have riveted our attention or caught our fancy."

Zippo was the brainchild of George Blaisdell, who wanted to replace unreliable matches and cumbersome lighters with a convenient, windproof gadget. Blaisdell liked the sound of the word zipper, another American invention, and the Zippo Manufacturing Co. was born in 1932.

The flattened chrome-plated brass cylinder has survived barely changed to this day, and the disposable lighters still carry a lifetime guarantee. But Zippos soon came in different finishes, imprinted with designs and logos of companies that wanted promotional souvenirs to give away, especially to foreigners.

In fact, Zippomania first made it big in the late 1980s in Japan, where the first books on the lighter appeared -- in English -- and found their way to the United States, helping to set the worldwide collector market on fire.

Japanese dealers snapped up of Zippos at trade and collectibles shows in the United States, pushing prices up to new highs. Zippos' cameo roles in movies such as "Apocalypse Now," "Lethal Weapon" and "Top Gun" added fuel to the fire.

The first Zippo lighters, which sold for $1.95, are now worth $8,000 to $10,000 -- if you can find them. Town and Country Sports models, considered to be the most beautiful and desirable Zippo series ever produced, are in this class.
"Some are worth $20,000 or $30,000. Most good pieces are worth at least $500 each," Poore said.

Even if you can find that rare piece, dislodging it from the holder may be impossible. Edward Fingerman, a collector for seven years, has turned down a $5,000 offer for early hand-enameled prototype Zippos.
A model featuring a whimsical picture of a tipsy man against a lamppost, now called "The Drunkard" by collectors, last sold for $4,000, Fingerman said.

Of the new models, the most expensive is $15,000 for a gold and silver inlaid, hand-engraved Zippo. Thirty-three such lighters were commissioned by Zippo in 1995, each with totally different designs. A dozen are still available from the company.
For those with smaller budgets, silver- or gold-plated Zippos cost $40 to $60, while those with sterling silver cases cost $179.

But don't spurn run-of-the-mill Zippos, which may some day be worth more than their $13 price now. Collectors zero in themes and will pay a premium to enlarge their portfolios based, for example, on taxis, food companies, American presidents and sports figures.
A $10 Zippo would be worth about $50 if it had a design that adds to a collector's private museum, which in some cases take up a whole living room or several safety deposit boxes.
For more information, call Zippo at 814-368-2700, or contact clubs such as On the Lighter Side (903-763-2795) and the Pocket Lighter Preservation Guild & Historical Society in Addison, Ill.
